It means the derelict site behind the market square that has been fenced off for eleven years finally being brought back into use. I do want to press the Minister on the mechanics of the fund, because the design matters as much as the sum. Bidding rounds favour authorities with the capacity to write bids. The councils that most need this money are frequently the ones that have lost the most planning and regeneration staff over the last decade, and they are being asked to compete against neighbours who retained that capacity. If we are serious about levelling up, we should be levelling up the ability to apply, not simply the pot applied for. I would also ask for clarity on timescales. Capital allocations that must be spent within a single financial year push authorities towards resurfacing and street furniture rather than the structural interventions that change a local economy. Give councils a five-year horizon and they will plan properly. Give them twelve months and they will buy planters. Finally, this fund cannot be a substitute for restoring core revenue funding. A refurbished high street with no libraries, no youth service and no social care behind it is a stage set, not a recovery, and our constituents will see through it quickly.

I mention her not out of sentiment, though there is plenty of that, but because she is the reason I keep returning to the question that sits underneath this bill. What kind of institution will she inherit if she ever does walk through those doors as something other than a visitor? Every decision we take about how we conduct ourselves here, about the tone we adopt across the aisle, about whether we treat a difficult vote as an argument to be won or an opponent to be destroyed, is a decision about that inheritance. I have watched the temperature in this chamber rise over the years I have served. I have contributed to it more often than I would like to admit. It is easy in the moment. A sharp line gets a clip, a clip gets shared, and the substance of what we were actually debating disappears entirely. Meanwhile the file in front of us goes unimproved. The measure before us today is not perfect. I have said so to the minister privately and I will say so publicly. But it is better than what preceded it, and it is better in part because members from three parties sat down in committee and did the unglamorous work of amendment. That happened. It does not get reported, but it happened, and it should happen more. So when I vote this evening I will be voting for the substance, and I will be voting with the awareness that my daughter, who currently believes that the most interesting thing about this building is that one can dress up as the Speaker, may one day read the record of what we said and how we said it. I would like that record to show that we were capable of disagreeing well. That is not a small thing to ask of ourselves.

felt on this question long after the cameras moved elsewhere, and that persistence deserves recognition, because the hardest thing in foreign policy is sustained attention. Conflicts do not end when they stop being novel. Syria has now endured more than a decade of war, and the pattern we see is one that should trouble anyone who cares about the international system. Chemical weapons were used against civilians. Hospitals were struck deliberately and repeatedly. Sieges were employed as a method of warfare. And the mechanisms that exist precisely to address such acts were blocked, vetoed, and worn down by attrition until the expectation of accountability faded. That fading is itself a harm, and it extends well beyond Syria's borders. Every commander watching in another theatre draws the obvious lesson. So let me set out what I believe we should be doing. First, we should continue to fund the evidence-gathering bodies, unglamorous as that work is, because prosecutions ten and twenty years from now will depend on documentation preserved today. Second, we should use universal jurisdiction where our own courts permit it, and we should resource those cases properly rather than announcing them and starving them. Third, on the humanitarian side, cross-border aid access cannot be treated as a bargaining chip renewed grudgingly every few months. Millions depend on those crossings, and the annual brinkmanship over their renewal is a disgrace. Fourth, we must be honest about reconstruction. There will be pressure to normalise relations and to fund rebuilding without any political settlement or accountability. I understand the humanitarian argument for it and I do not dismiss it, but rebuilding a country for the government that destroyed it, with no guarantee of safe return for those it displaced, is not reconstruction. It is ratification. I would welcome the Minister setting out the Government's position on that last point specifically, because it is the question that will define the next phase.

as someone who has spent a good deal of time looking at how these plans actually translate into services on the ground, I want to offer a note of caution alongside my welcome. Local transport plans are extremely good documents. They are well written, they contain maps, they set out modal shift targets with commendable precision, and a great many of them sit on shelves. The gap between the plan and the bus is where the public loses faith, and it is where we as legislators ought to be concentrating. Take active travel. Every plan of the last decade has promised a coherent cycling network. What has typically been delivered is a series of disconnected fragments, painted lanes that end abruptly at the point where the road narrows and the difficulty begins, precisely where the infrastructure is most needed. A network that is safe for ninety per cent of a journey is not safe. Parents assessing whether their child can cycle to school assess the worst hundred metres, not the average. Until funding is structured around completed routes rather than delivered kilometres, we will keep buying fragments. On buses, the picture is starker. Deregulation left us with commercial operators cherry-picking profitable corridors while the authority is left to subsidise the rest from a shrinking pot. Franchising offers a route out of that, but it is expensive, legally fraught, and takes years, and smaller authorities have neither the money nor the specialist staff to attempt it. If the Government genuinely wants reform, it should meet the transition costs directly rather than praising the ambition and leaving the bill locally. And on low carbon solutions, I would gently observe that electrifying a fleet that nobody rides achieves very little. Patronage first, propulsion second. Get the frequency and the reliability right, and the environmental case makes itself, because the alternative to a good bus is a car, not a better bus.

distortions that come with distance. When an event passes out of living memory, it passes into the hands of those who would edit it. We are approaching that threshold now. The number of people alive who can say I was there, I saw it, this is what happened to my family is falling every year, and within a decade there will be almost none. What replaces direct testimony is contested ground, and we can already see who intends to contest it. I want to be careful here, because there is a serious argument against legislating in this area and it deserves an answer rather than a dismissal. The argument runs that historical truth should be established by historians and by evidence, not by statute, and that criminalising falsehood risks giving the falsifier the status of a martyr while doing nothing to change a single mind. I take that seriously. I have seen prosecutions produce exactly that effect. But I do not think it settles the matter, for two reasons. The first is that denial is not ordinarily an error about history. It is a contemporary political act that uses historical claims as its instrument, and its purpose is to rehabilitate the ideology that produced the camps. The second is that we already accept limits on expression where speech operates as incitement or as harassment directed at an identifiable group, and denial functions in precisely that way for the descendants of those who were murdered. What I would ask of those drafting this measure is precision. The offence must be tightly drawn around deliberate falsification and diminishment, with clear protection for genuine scholarship, including scholarship that revises figures or challenges established accounts on the basis of evidence. History must remain arguable. What must not remain arguable is whether it happened. And alongside the law, the education must continue, because a prosecution teaches nobody, and a classroom teaches everybody.

In Cumbria we are not naturally given to deference, and we are quick to detect anything performed rather than meant. He passed that test comfortably. What comes back to me from constituents over these last days is not the ceremonial. It is the practical. It is the Duke of Edinburgh's award, which in a rural county like mine has taken thousands of young people onto the fells with a map and a heavy pack and brought them back with something they did not have before. I have met farmers in their sixties who still talk about their expedition, who can name the route and the weather and the person who nearly gave up at Kirkstone. That scheme understood something that a great deal of modern youth policy misses. It did not ask young people to discuss their potential. It asked them to walk twenty miles and cook their own dinner, and it let the confidence follow from the doing. Its reach is remarkable. It runs in more than a hundred countries. It has adapted to young people in secure units, in care, in circumstances entirely unlike those of the boys it was designed for in 1956. That adaptability is a form of humility on the part of its founder, a willingness to let the thing outgrow him. There is his work on conservation too, taken up long before it was fashionable and at some cost to his reputation among those who thought a royal duke should stick to ribbon-cutting. He did not stick to ribbon-cutting. He had opinions, he expressed them, and he was occasionally wrong in public, which is a great deal more than most public figures risk. My constituents send their condolences to Her Majesty and to the family, with genuine warmth and no ceremony at all, which I suspect he would have preferred.

They had not been taught. That is the thing he kept coming back to afterwards. His frustration was not directed at those young people. It was directed at a system that sent them into adulthood without the most basic account of the country they live in, and then left it to the few indigenous kids in the room to do the explaining, over and over, at whatever cost to themselves. I want members to sit with that for a moment, because it describes a burden we impose without ever naming it. The child who has to explain residential schools to their classmates is doing unpaid work. The adult who has to explain the sixties scoop to a colleague at a staff meeting is doing unpaid work. And the emotional cost of that work is highest for the people least equipped to absorb it, because the history in question is their own family's, not an abstraction from a textbook. This is why curriculum matters so much, and why I keep raising it despite the jurisdictional complications that members opposite are entirely correct to point out. Yes, education is provincial. That is a reason to convene, to fund, to develop materials in partnership with nations and to make them freely available, not a reason to fold our arms. We have found ways to act nationally on plenty of provincial matters when the will existed. What my son needed in that room was not a better answer of his own. He had the answer. What he needed was for the question to have been asked of everyone else, years earlier, by someone whose job it was to ask it. We can arrange that. It is entirely within our power.

hardest part of this is not the announcement, it is the six months after the announcement, when the attention has moved on and the delivery has to happen anyway. That is where governments of every colour have historically come unstuck, and I say that as someone who has served in one. So let me set out the three things I will be watching. First, capacity. It is one thing to publish a target and quite another to have the people, the buildings and the equipment to meet it. I would like the Minister to tell the House what workforce assumptions sit behind yesterday's figures. If the answer is that existing staff will absorb the additional work through improved productivity, then we should say so plainly, and we should expect the backlog elsewhere to grow accordingly. There is no free capacity in the system. Anyone who has visited a hospital or a jobcentre or a courthouse in the last year knows that. Second, data. We cannot manage what we do not measure, and at present the reporting is patchy, lagged and in several places collected differently in different regions, which makes comparison impossible. A published monthly dataset, at local authority level, with the methodology set out, would do more for public confidence than another dispatch box statement. It would also allow this House to hold the Government to account with facts rather than anecdote, which I would have thought was in everybody's interest. Third, the exit. Every emergency measure needs a defined end point and a test for reaching it. Powers taken in a crisis have a habit of settling in and becoming ordinary. I do not attribute bad motives to anyone in that. It is simply easier to keep a power than to give it up. But this House should insist on sunset provisions with real teeth, and on a proper vote rather than a technical renewal slipped through on a Thursday afternoon.

That is the crux of it, and it is worth dwelling on why we were able to say it with some confidence. We did not begin from a preferred answer. We began by modelling what actually happens to each authority's income under four different scenarios, and we published the underlying spreadsheet so that others could check us. I would encourage every member with doubts to look at their own area's line in that table. Several colleagues who came to us convinced their council would lose out discovered the opposite. Now, the practicality argument. Critics say this is a decade-long reform being presented as a two-year one. I understand the scepticism, because we have all watched revaluation cycles slip. But the mechanism we propose does not require new primary legislation for each step. It requires one enabling measure, then administrative implementation through existing channels, with an annual reconciliation. The Valuation Office has confirmed to us that the data requirements are within reach of its current systems, provided the timetable for revaluation is not simultaneously compressed. That caveat matters and I put it on the record. What we cannot do is nothing. The present system taxes the physical presence of a business at exactly the moment when physical presence is what our town centres are desperate to retain. A retailer with a shopfront pays. A competitor with a distribution shed and a website pays a fraction. Whatever one thinks of our particular remedy, that asymmetry is indefensible and it is actively hollowing out the places we all represent. I would rather this House argued about the design of a replacement than spent another parliament agreeing that the current arrangement is unsatisfactory while leaving it precisely as it is.

That certainty has been in short supply for four years, and businesses have paid for the shortage in cancelled investment, in stockpiling costs, in staff time spent on contingency planning that turned out to be wasted, and in the simple exhaustion of not being able to plan beyond the next deadline. I meet manufacturers who have redesigned their supply chains twice and are now being asked to consider doing it a third time. There is a limit to how often you can ask that of people who are trying to run a business. On unfettered access, let me be precise about what businesses actually need, because the phrase is used loosely. They need to know that goods placed on the market in Northern Ireland can move to Great Britain without new declarations, without new checks, and without a compliance function that a firm of eleven people cannot possibly staff. They need that in a form that survives a change of minister. And they need the same clarity in the other direction, which is where the real difficulty lies and where I would like to hear rather more from the Government than we have had. The traffic that worries my constituents is not the traffic leaving Northern Ireland. It is the supermarket lorry arriving. I will support the Bill because the alternative on offer is worse, but supporting it does not require pretending it is elegant. It is a repair to a structure that was designed in haste under time pressure by people who knew at the time that it contained an unresolved contradiction. That contradiction has not gone away because we have legislated around it. What would help now is less commentary about who said what and more sustained, quiet negotiation with the Commission, conducted away from microphones, by people who are willing to bank a partial solution rather than hold out for a total one. That is how these things get settled.

It is absurd that in 2021 a driver may need four separate apps, three RFID cards and an account with each network in order to be confident of charging on a two-hundred-mile journey. Nobody accepts this at a petrol station. You arrive, you pay by card, you leave. Contactless payment should be mandatory on every new rapid charger without exception, and retrofitted to existing ones on a defined timetable. The second is reliability, and I regard this as the sleeper issue. A charger that exists on a map but does not work is worse than no charger at all, because the driver has planned around it. We have no reliable public data on uptime. Operators know their own figures and do not publish them. I would like the Government to mandate the publication of uptime statistics per site, in a standard format, so that a driver can see before setting off which network actually maintains its equipment. Market discipline requires information, and at present there is none. The third is equity, and it is the one I feel most strongly about. Roughly a third of households have no off-street parking. Those households currently pay a substantially higher rate of VAT on public charging than a homeowner pays on domestic electricity, and they pay a higher unit price on top. We have therefore constructed a system in which the people least able to afford an electric vehicle face the highest running costs. That will not survive contact with the public once volumes rise, and we should fix it now rather than after it becomes a grievance. Lamp-post charging, cross-pavement channels and a sensible planning regime for on-street provision all help, but the tax anomaly is the thing only this House can address.

disabilities face every day in this State, and I want to be careful that we do not allow the ceremony of ratification to substitute for the substance of change. We have a long habit of that. We sign the instrument, we issue the statement, we take the photograph, and the person waiting four years for a wheelchair assessment waits a fifth. Let me put some specifics on the record. Personal assistance hours are rationed on the basis of budget rather than assessed need, and the assessment itself is frequently conducted by the body that will have to pay for the outcome. That is a structural conflict and everybody involved knows it. Education services are provided late and litigated often, so that parents who should be raising a child are instead assembling legal files. Transport in rural areas is effectively unavailable, which means employment is effectively unavailable, which means the poverty statistics for disabled people in this country look the way they do. And the deprivation of liberty provisions, which the convention speaks to directly, remain unresolved in our law despite repeated commitments. Ratification places obligations on us in each of those areas. It also creates a reporting cycle, and I want to ask the Minister of State a direct question about that. Will the State's periodic reports be laid before this House and debated, or will they be filed in Geneva and never discussed here? Because the value of the convention lies almost entirely in the pressure the reporting cycle generates, and pressure requires an audience. I would also press him on the optional protocol. Ratifying the convention without the protocol means an individual whose rights are breached has no route to complain internationally. It removes the enforcement and keeps the aspiration, and I think people with disabilities in this country have had quite enough aspiration. Nothing about us without us was the slogan of this campaign. It should now become the operating method of the Department.

The petitioners are not fisheries scientists. They are people who have watched a river they grew up beside empty out within a single working lifetime. On the Fraser system, returns in recent years have been the lowest on record. Some runs are now measured in the hundreds where they were once measured in the hundreds of thousands. The Big Bar landslide compounded it, and the response to that slide, however well intentioned, was slow enough that fish died at the base of it while procurement processes ran their course. My constituents want three things. They want open-net pen aquaculture removed from wild migration routes on the timetable that was promised, not the timetable that has been quietly extended. They want habitat restoration funded at a scale that matches the damage, which means culverts, side channels and riparian planting across hundreds of small watersheds, not a handful of showcase projects. And they want the science branch of the department to be structurally independent of the licensing branch, so that when the advice is inconvenient it is still published. I want to say something about the First Nations dimension as well, because it runs through every part of this. Communities in my region have voluntarily forgone food, social and ceremonial fisheries for several seasons now. They have absorbed a cost that no other user group has been asked to absorb, and they have done it to give the fish a chance. The least they are owed is a genuine role in management decisions rather than consultation conducted after the decision has been drafted. I present this petition on their behalf and on behalf of the commercial and recreational fishers who, unusually, find themselves in complete agreement.

I have heard that point made forcefully by hauliers in her constituency and in mine. The difficulty I face is one of headroom. Excise on this fuel is not simply a revenue line; it is a revenue line against which a substantial part of current expenditure is already committed. Every cent removed costs the Exchequer in the order of tens of millions in a full year, and if the reduction is to be sustained rather than temporary, that money must be found from somewhere else or borrowed. I am not making an argument against acting. I am making an argument for honesty about what acting costs. There is also the question of pass-through. When we reduced the rate, we monitored forecourt prices closely, and in the main the reduction did reach the pump, though not everywhere and not immediately. I would say to any retailer tempted to absorb a reduction into margin that we are watching, and that the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission has been asked to take an interest. On the medium term, the Deputy and I both know that this cannot be the permanent policy. Excise on transport fuels is a declining base for reasons we have collectively legislated for, and we will at some point need an honest conversation in this House about what replaces it. Road pricing is the obvious candidate and it is politically radioactive, which is precisely why no government has begun the work. I would rather begin it now, with a commission and a long lead time, than face it as an emergency in eight years. In the immediate term, I will keep the position under review at each fiscal event, and I will engage with the sector directly on the rebate mechanism.

position is not born of constitutional preference alone. It rests on a straightforward observation about how avoidance actually works. The schemes that concern us are not designed in Scotland or England. They are designed by a small number of firms operating internationally, and they exploit the interaction between jurisdictions rather than the rules of any one of them. Devolving a power to Scotland would not, on its own, close a structure that routes through three other countries. I accept that, and I would rather say so than overclaim. What devolution would deliver is a different appetite for enforcement. Resourcing is the whole game here. Every credible study finds that additional investment in compliance staff returns several times its cost, and yet the headcount devoted to the most complex cases has fallen over the last decade while the complexity has risen. That is a choice, and it is a choice made here. So let me put four specific asks to the Minister, none of which requires a constitutional argument. First, publish the tax gap broken down by behaviour and by taxpayer segment, annually, with the methodology open to scrutiny. Second, commit to a minimum number of specialist investigators for large and complex cases and report against it. Third, bring forward the register of overseas entities with meaningful verification rather than self-declaration, because a register that nobody checks is a filing cabinet. Fourth, act on the enablers. Individual avoidance schemes are whack-a-mole, but the firms marketing them are a finite and identifiable population, and penalties that bite on the promoter rather than the participant would change behaviour far faster. If the Government moves on those four, my colleagues and I will support it and say so publicly. If it does not, we will continue to make the case that these powers would be exercised more seriously elsewhere, and the Minister will find that the argument gets easier for us to make with every year that the compliance headcount falls.

That is the lesson I would draw and I want to press it, because it is easy to admire an emergency response and hard to fund the ordinary infrastructure that made the response possible. The advice line did not appear from nowhere. It was built on a welfare rights service that had been maintained through a decade in which maintaining it was neither cheap nor politically rewarded. The distribution network relied on community centres that had been kept open, and on staff who knew which streets to reach first. Cut those things in the good years and the response in the bad years is a press release. I want to mention the free school meals question specifically. During the school closures, the difference between areas that provided food directly and areas that issued vouchers was substantial, and it fell hardest on families without reliable internet access or a smartphone, who could not redeem a voucher they could not download. Digital-by-default administration was already excluding people before the pandemic. The pandemic simply made the exclusion visible and urgent. I would ask the Minister what assessment has been made of that, and whether the lesson has been carried into current programme design or filed away with the other lessons. There is also a devolution point here that I make without rancour. Cardiff was able to act at pace partly because decisions about school food sat close to the people making them. That proximity is worth something. Where responsibility is fragmented across three levels of government, each of which can plausibly point at another, the family waiting for a meal experiences that fragmentation as delay. Whatever our differences about where powers should sit, we should be able to agree that they should sit somewhere identifiable.

I still have the book somewhere, with the entries written in by hand. My point in telling that story is not nostalgia, though I confess to a fair amount of it. It is that the branch on the corner did something a screen cannot do. The woman behind the counter knew my mother, knew our circumstances, and would have noticed if something changed. That noticing is what we have lost, and it turns out to have been doing more work than we understood. Consider fraud. The overwhelming majority of the cases I deal with in my constituency office involve older people persuaded to move money at speed by someone on the telephone. In a branch, that transaction meets a human being who has been trained to ask why. Online, it meets nothing at all. The banks' own figures show that in-branch interventions stop a substantial volume of attempted fraud every year, and yet the branches continue to close on the basis of transaction counts that take no account of the transactions prevented. Consider also cash. About one in ten adults in this part of the world relies on cash for day-to-day spending, and the proportion is far higher among those on the lowest incomes, for whom cash is a budgeting tool rather than a preference. Telling those people that the market has moved on is telling them that the market has moved on without them. The post office network absorbs some of this, and I pay tribute to the postmasters who have taken it on, but they are being asked to provide banking services on commission rates that do not cover the cost of the insurance, let alone the staff time. So my ask of the Minister is modest. Before a bank may close its last branch in a town, require a genuine assessment of local need, published, with a right of appeal. That is not a heavy imposition on an institution reporting the profits these institutions report.

the dispute settlement mechanism, I would say to the member that he is describing a change in form and calling it a change in substance. The previous mechanism was, in practice, unavailable to us, because it could be blocked by the very party against whom we sought to invoke it. A remedy that the other side can veto is not a remedy. What we have secured is a panel process that cannot be frustrated in that way, with defined timelines and with the roster arrangements settled in advance precisely so that appointments cannot be stalled. That is a substantive gain and I am happy to defend it in detail at committee. On aluminum specifically, since the member returned to it, let me repeat the figures because they matter. Seventy per cent of the aluminum purchased by manufacturers must now originate in North America. That requirement did not exist before. It was fought for by our negotiators at the request of the industry and of the workers in that industry, and it was not conceded willingly by the other side. I have heard the criticism that we should have secured a smelted-and-poured definition from the outset rather than on the timeline agreed. That criticism is fair and I will not pretend otherwise. Our position is that we secured the definition, that it applies from the date agreed, and that in the interim the origin requirement itself provides real protection. The member may judge that insufficient. What he cannot reasonably claim is that nothing was obtained. Negotiation involves an opposite party who wants different things and who has more leverage than we would prefer. The test is not whether we achieved everything the sector asked for. The test is whether we achieved more than the alternative on the table, which was termination of the agreement altogether, with tariff exposure across every sector represented by members in this chamber. I believe we did, and the industry associations have said so themselves.

has had a devastating impact on the finances of Luton Borough Council, principally because of the collapse in income from London Luton Airport, which the council owns and from which it has historically funded a substantial share of its services. Passenger numbers fell by more than three quarters. The dividend that paid for children's services, for adult social care, for parks and libraries, simply stopped. Now, I have heard it suggested that this is a consequence of the council having taken a commercial risk. I want to address that directly, because it is unfair. Luton did not speculate on office blocks in another region or buy a shopping centre two hundred miles away. It owns and operates the airport that sits within its boundary, an asset it has held for decades, integral to the local economy and employing thousands of local residents. The council did precisely what successive governments have urged local authorities to do, which is to reduce dependence on central grant by developing its own income. It was praised for it. To be told now that the resulting exposure is its own affair is to change the terms after the fact. The consequence is a budget gap of tens of millions and a set of cuts that no councillor of any party wanted to make. Youth services gone. Library hours reduced. Charges introduced where none existed. And these fall on a town with significant deprivation, where the residents affected have no relationship whatsoever to the aviation market. The petitioners therefore request that the House urge the Government to provide compensation for irrecoverable income losses arising from the pandemic, on the same principle applied to other public bodies, and to review the treatment of commercial income within the local government finance settlement so that authorities are not penalised for having followed the advice they were given. I commend the petition to the House.

conflicting statements about the future of services at the hospital within a matter of weeks, and neither statement has been withdrawn. Staff read both. Patients read both. Nobody can tell me which one currently represents policy. That is not a communications failure, it is a governance failure, and it tells us something about how decisions of this magnitude are being taken. Let me set out the sequence for the record. In the spring, a service plan was circulated internally indicating a reconfiguration. When that became public, it was described as a draft with no status. In the summer, staffing was reduced in a manner entirely consistent with the draft that had no status. Rotas were not filled. Locum cover was arranged on a month-to-month basis, which anyone who has worked in a hospital will tell you is how a department is closed without anybody having to announce a closure. Then came the letter to which I referred. I have seen this pattern before in other parts of the country and it follows a reliable script. The service is run down until it becomes genuinely unsafe, at which point safety is cited as the reason for the change that the running-down was designed to produce. Nobody has to defend the original decision because the original decision is never formally taken. I am asking the Minister for two commitments. First, that no permanent change to the configuration of services at this hospital will proceed without a published review, a defined consultation period, and a formal decision that a Minister is prepared to defend in this House. Second, that recruitment to the permanent posts currently being covered by locums resumes immediately, because as long as those posts remain unfilled the outcome is being determined by attrition rather than by policy. The people I represent are entitled to know what is planned for their hospital. At present they are being asked to infer it from the rota.

I say it because the scheduling of a debate is itself a statement about how seriously the subject is taken, and the people affected by this issue notice where in the day it lands. They watch the feed. They see the empty benches. They draw the obvious conclusion, and it is not an unreasonable one. So let me try to use the time properly rather than complain about it. The core difficulty here is that responsibility is distributed across three Departments and an agency, and that the funding follows a different logic in each. When a family comes to my office, they are not experiencing a policy area. They are experiencing a series of doors, each of which opens onto a person who is helpful, sympathetic, and unable to act because the relevant budget line sits elsewhere. That is the actual mechanism of failure, and it is remarkably resistant to statements of intent. What would fix it is not more strategy documents. It is a single accountable office with a budget of its own and the authority to direct, and a named official who can be brought before a committee and asked what happened in a specific case. We have created such structures before when the political will existed. The absence here is not capability, it is priority. I would also make a point about data. They have increased spending in the middle of an inflationary episode, financed a substantial share of it through borrowing, and then expressed puzzlement at the price level. I want to be fair about the parts of this that are genuinely not the government's doing. Global energy prices moved for reasons entirely outside Ottawa's control. Supply chains seized up worldwide. Every advanced economy is dealing with some version of this, and any member who claims their party would have delivered two per cent inflation through the last three years is not being straight with the public. But that concession does not get the government to where it wants to be, because the question is never whether external shocks occurred. It is what a government does in response, and this one chose to add demand to an economy that was already supply-constrained, and to do so through programs designed for a downturn rather than for an overheating. The carbon levy is the clearest example of a self-inflicted component. I understand the theory. Price the externality, return the revenue, let households adjust. But in my riding there is no bus, the nearest hospital is an hour's drive, and the heating season lasts seven months. The behavioural adjustment the theory assumes is not available. So the levy functions as a straightforward transfer out of rural households, and the rebate, whatever the modelling says on average, does not restore the households I represent, because averages conceal exactly the variation that matters here. What I would ask for is not the abolition of every measure but an honest accounting. Publish the distributional analysis by community size and by heating type, not by province. Publish the estimate of the levy's contribution to headline inflation, which the government's own bank has produced and which ministers decline to quote. Let people see the numbers and decide. If the policy is as benign as the government claims, transparency costs it nothing.

That is the point I am making, and I want to develop it because I think Members have taken it as a piece of provocation rather than as an argument. The convention that the monarch does not intervene in political decisions is not written down in any statute we could amend. It is a habit, maintained by individuals, some of whom have found it inconvenient. It held during the abdication crisis because the government of the day was prepared to force the issue and because the individual concerned was, in the end, more interested in the marriage than in the throne. Had he been more interested in the throne, and had he been willing to use the residual powers that were arguably still available, the constitutional position would have been tested in circumstances of extraordinary danger. We were fortunate. Constitutional arrangements that depend on fortune are arrangements we should examine when there is no crisis, which is to say now. I am not arguing for abolition. I am arguing that where discretionary powers exist without a written constraint, we should write the constraint down while the question is academic, because the moment it ceases to be academic is precisely the moment when agreement becomes impossible. The prorogation episode demonstrated this. A power everyone assumed was formal turned out to be substantive when someone chose to use it substantively, and the resolution had to be improvised by a court under enormous pressure in a matter of weeks. That is a poor way to settle fundamental questions. So the amendment I am supporting is modest. It asks that the exercise of these powers be placed on a statutory footing with defined conditions. That is not radical. It is what almost every comparable democracy has already done, and none of them has come to any harm from it.

A trolley in a corridor is the visible end of a chain that begins with a person who cannot be discharged because the home support package is not available, occupies a bed that the medical patient needs, who then waits in the emergency department, which then cannot accept the ambulance, which then cannot respond to the call. Every one of those links is a capacity decision taken years earlier. On the private hospital arrangement, I want to be honest about the limitations, because I was closely involved in the negotiation of the earlier agreement and I would not repeat it in the same form. Paying for capacity in the aggregate, whether or not it is used, gave us certainty and gave us poor value, because the consultants who work in those facilities largely also work in ours, and we ended up in some instances renting a building whose staff we were already employing. Any future arrangement must be activity-based, must specify the procedures to be delivered, and must include the workforce, or we will simply move the same doctors between two sets of premises at greater cost. On primary care, the Deputy and I agree more than we disagree. The community intervention teams and the integrated care programmes for older persons do work where they are properly staffed, and the evidence on avoided admissions is good. The constraint is again staffing, and specifically the differential between what a nurse can earn in the community sector and in the acute sector, which we created ourselves and which we could close. I have asked officials for costings on that, and I will bring them to the House when I have them rather than announce a figure I cannot stand over.

She is ninety-three. She was eleven when she was deported. She spoke for forty minutes without notes, and what struck me was not the horror of what she described, though it was horrific, but the specificity. She remembered the name of the girl who shared her bunk. She remembered what the guard's dog was called. She remembered that on the day of the selection she was wearing shoes that did not fit and worried about it, because an eleven-year-old worries about her shoes. That specificity is what defeats abstraction, and abstraction is how six million becomes a number rather than six million individual endings. There will not be many more such visits. Within a few years there will be no one left who can say I was there. What we do about that is the question this House should be considering, and I do not think we have an adequate answer yet. Recording testimony is necessary but a recording is not a person in a room, and every teacher will tell you the difference in how the class listens. So we need to think about the second generation, about the descendants who carry the accounts, and about how we equip them to bear a responsibility they did not ask for. We also need to be clear-eyed about the present. Antisemitic incidents in this country have risen year on year for most of the last decade. Jewish schools require security that no other school requires, funded in part by the community itself. Synagogues have guards. That is the situation now, in Britain, and remembrance that does not connect the past to that present is a ceremony rather than a commitment. I would rather we made the connection explicitly, uncomfortable as it is.

When the maximum is derisory, marginal cases are not brought, because the cost of a contested trial cannot be justified against an outcome of a few weeks. So the low maximum does not merely produce lenient sentences in the cases that reach court. It reduces the number of cases that reach court at all, and the pattern of offending that we then measure appears smaller than it is. Raising the maximum to five years does three things. It allows the court to reflect genuine gravity in the worst cases. It makes the offence triable in a way that unlocks investigative powers currently unavailable. And it changes the calculation for the person considering whether the risk is worth taking, which is the only form of prevention that operates before the animal is harmed rather than after. The approach currently applied evaluates a medicine against a cost-effectiveness threshold that has not been revised in over a decade and which was, when set, an administrative convenience rather than an empirically derived figure. It has since acquired the status of a scientific constant. It is not one. Holding it fixed in nominal terms through a period of substantial inflation has quietly tightened the criterion year after year without any decision being taken to tighten it, which is a strange way to make policy on something this consequential. The second difficulty is the treatment of uncertainty. For rare disease medicines, the trial population is by definition small, the follow-up is short, and the long-term extrapolation is therefore wide. The current approach penalises that uncertainty by taking a conservative estimate at each step, and because the steps compound, the result is systematically pessimistic in a way that nobody intends and everyone in the process privately acknowledges. Managed access agreements exist precisely to handle this, by funding provisionally while the data matures, and we use them far less than comparable health systems. Third, the negotiating position. Because the assessment is conducted before rather than alongside the commercial discussion, the State arrives with a public reservation price. Any negotiator will tell you what that does. I would draw the Minister's attention to the arrangements in operation in several other member states where the two processes run in parallel with confidential net pricing, and where time from authorisation to reimbursement is roughly half of ours. I am not suggesting we import a system wholesale. I am suggesting that a two-year median delay, during which people with progressive conditions deteriorate irreversibly, is not a defensible outcome, and that the review promised eighteen months ago should be published rather than pending.

Let me identify the three that concern me most. The first is prominence. A settlement negotiated in a rush, announced without a published methodology, and then frozen in nominal terms, is a real-terms reduction whose size is determined by inflation rather than by any assessment of what the service should provide. If we wish the broadcaster to do less, we should say which things and take responsibility for the choice. Determining it by arithmetic allows us to will the reduction while deploring its consequences, which is a habit this House should try to break. The third is regional production, which matters enormously to constituencies like mine. Quotas have shifted a substantial volume of production out of London, and that has created genuine skilled employment in places that had none. reminds us that by wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established. Both verses came to my mind this week, and I want to explain why rather than simply quote them. Integrity of heart and skilful hands are two different qualities and they do not often reside in the same person. Plenty of public figures have one. The rarity is the combination, and the reason the second is required is that good intentions unaccompanied by competence produce a great deal of damage. What we have observed over seventy years is a technical mastery of a role that most people underestimate precisely because it is performed without apparent effort. Consider the weekly audience. Fifteen prime ministers, of every political persuasion, several of whom arrived in office with no particular affection for the institution, and every one of them left a record describing the same experience of being questioned by someone who had read the papers thoroughly. That is skilful hands. Consider the discipline of never once, in seven decades, allowing a personal political view to become public, in an era in which every person in public life is invited hourly to comment on everything. I do not know whether Members appreciate how difficult that is. I have managed it for about a fortnight at a time. And consider the visits to Ireland and to Northern Ireland, undertaken at a moment when they carried real risk and real symbolic weight, and executed with a judgment about tone that no adviser could have supplied. That was not ceremony. That was statecraft conducted through gesture, and it moved things that speeches had not moved. For my constituents, the connection is more personal and less analytical. It is a photograph on a mantelpiece from a visit in 1977. It is a letter received on a hundredth birthday. It is a constancy that spanned their entire lives. We give thanks for that service, and we pray for the family in their grief.

The scheme requires an application. Every scheme that requires an application has a take-up rate below one hundred per cent, and the shortfall is never randomly distributed. It concentrates among the people the scheme was designed for, because they are the ones without the broadband connection, the documentation, the confident English, or the time. We have decades of evidence on this. Pension credit take-up has hovered around two thirds for as long as I have been in this House. So my first question to the Department is whether any part of this can be paid automatically on the basis of data already held. Where an individual is already in receipt of a qualifying benefit, the Department knows who they are and knows their bank details, and requiring them to apply serves no purpose except to reduce the number who receive the money. If that is the intention, we should say so. If it is not, automation is available. My second concern is the appeals route. The impact assessment assumes a certain error rate at initial decision, and history suggests the assumption is optimistic. If an applicant is wrongly refused, what is the route to challenge, how long does it take, and is there any interim payment while the challenge proceeds? An appeal that resolves in fourteen weeks is no use to a household that cannot pay a bill in three. Third, the interaction with existing entitlements. If this payment counts as income for the purposes of another means test, then a proportion of recipients will gain with one hand and lose with the other, and will be understandably furious about it. I would be grateful if the Minister could confirm at the Dispatch Box today that the payment is disregarded across the board, because the guidance published so far is silent on it.

Act requires me to come before the House annually and make the case afresh, and I want to acknowledge that some Deputies regard that annual exercise as having become a formality. I understand the criticism and I do not think it is unreasonable. When a provision has been renewed every year for two decades, the renewal begins to look like permanence achieved by instalments, and the emergency character that justified the departure from ordinary procedure fades from view. So let me put the actual basis for my conclusion on the record rather than assert it. In the reporting period, the relevant provisions were invoked in a number of cases which I have set out in the memorandum circulated to Deputies, together with the outcomes. The Garda authorities have provided an assessment of current organised crime activity which I have considered, and which indicates that the specific intimidation of witnesses and jurors that these provisions were designed to address remains an operational reality rather than a historical one. I have also considered the report of the independent reviewer, who identifies two areas where practice has drifted from what the legislation contemplated and recommends corrective guidance. I have accepted both recommendations and the guidance will issue this term. What I would say to the House is that the group's final report, which I expect within the year, will give us the first genuine opportunity in a long time to consider whether these provisions should be normalised into the ordinary law with appropriate safeguards, sunsetted properly, or retained as they are. I do not intend to prejudge that. What I will undertake is that the report will be published in full, that time will be provided for a substantive debate on it rather than a renewal motion, and that any legislative response will go to pre-legislative scrutiny. Emergency provisions that survive twenty years deserve a proper examination at least once, and this House has not had one.

The overwhelming majority of foreign investment in this country is entirely legitimate, generates employment, and is welcome. Nothing in this legislation is aimed at it. What is aimed at is a specific and identifiable pattern, and I want to describe it because vagueness in this area helps only the people we are trying to reach. The pattern is the purchase of high-value property through a chain of corporate vehicles registered in jurisdictions that do not disclose beneficial ownership, financed by funds whose origin cannot be traced, held for long periods without occupation, and serviced by a professional ecosystem of lawyers, accountants and agents who ask a limited number of questions. Every element of that chain is currently lawful. That is the problem, and it is a problem we created through a succession of individually reasonable decisions about privacy and about competitiveness. The register of overseas entities addresses the first link. Unexplained wealth orders address the last resort. What sits between them, and what I think this Bill still treats too lightly, is the enabler question. A shell company does not incorporate itself. Somebody drafts the documents, somebody provides the registered address, and somebody signs off the source of funds. Those people are regulated professionals subject to supervisory bodies, and the enforcement record of several of those supervisory bodies is, to put it charitably, thin. I would like to see the Government take powers to consolidate that supervision and to publish enforcement statistics by firm. The second thing I would press for is resourcing. An unexplained wealth order costs a great deal to litigate against a respondent with unlimited funds, and the agencies have been deterred by adverse costs exposure. Cap that exposure and the tool becomes usable rather than symbolic.

The reality has moved on entirely. What we are dealing with now is industrial. Software acquires inventory within seconds of a general sale opening, at a scale no individual could achieve, and lists it on secondary platforms at multiples of face value within minutes. The genuine fan refreshing a browser was never in competition with another fan. They were in competition with a server farm. Several things follow from that. First, any remedy framed around the individual reseller misses the target. The person listing four tickets is not the problem, and legislation that catches them while leaving the automated operations untouched will be worse than useless, because it will generate enforcement activity against the visible and easy while the substantive harm continues. Second, the secondary platforms are not passive intermediaries. They take a commission on both sides of every transaction, which means their revenue rises directly with the markup, which means their commercial interest is aligned precisely against the outcome this Bill seeks. Any regulatory design that relies on their voluntary cooperation should be assessed with that in mind. Third, enforcement requires a named authority with resources and the ability to act against entities based abroad. Without that, we will pass a law that is admired and never applied, as has happened in other jurisdictions that legislated in this area and then declined to fund the follow-through. I would also ask the Minister to consider requiring that all tickets be sold with a mandatory identity or transfer mechanism for events above a certain size, since the technology exists, is in routine use elsewhere, and removes the resale value at source rather than attempting to police it afterwards. Prevention is considerably cheaper than prosecution here.

A wheelchair user travelling in one direction can board and cannot return. In practice this means the station is unusable, because journeys are round trips, and yet in the official statistics it counts as partially accessible, which is a category that flatters the network considerably. On invisible disabilities, the picture is different and in some ways harder. Physical adaptation is expensive but conceptually simple. You know when you have built a ramp. Accommodating a passenger with autism, or with a cognitive impairment, or with a fluctuating condition that means today is fine and tomorrow is not, requires staff who are present, trained and empowered to exercise judgment. All three of those have been reduced. Ticket office closures remove the person who would have helped. Automated announcements that change platform at short notice are manageable for most of us and genuinely disabling for some. The assistance booking system requires notice, and the requirement for notice is itself the discrimination, because nobody else has to plan a journey a day in advance. I want to acknowledge that operators have made progress and that some of the staff I have met are outstanding at this. The difficulty is that the quality depends entirely on who happens to be on shift, and a system whose accessibility depends on individual goodwill is not an accessible system. What we need is a statutory standard with enforcement behind it, a published compliance table by operator, and a passenger route to redress that does not require a solicitor. None of that is expensive relative to the capital programme.

Announcing a site is easy. Ensuring that the jobs created go to residents of the surrounding wards rather than to commuters from thirty miles away requires deliberate design, and it does not happen automatically. The evidence from previous rounds of this kind of intervention is fairly consistent. Where local employment obligations were written into the arrangements, with targets, monitoring and consequences, local employment followed. Where they were left to good intentions, the employment effect leaked out of the area within about eighteen months, and the residual benefit to the host community was the traffic. I would therefore urge the Minister to make training and recruitment commitments a condition rather than an aspiration, and to publish the outturn against them annually. The second thing that determines whether these sites succeed is transport, which I appreciate is not this Minister's brief but which cannot be separated from it. A distribution facility on a bypass with no bus service is accessible only to those with a car, and the households in greatest need of the work are least likely to have one. We have built employment sites in this configuration repeatedly and then wondered why the local unemployment rate did not shift. Third, skills. The qualifications required will not exist locally in sufficient numbers at the point the site opens, because the college needs three years of notice to build the provision and typically gets three months. I want to make the case for these stations as infrastructure rather than as a cultural amenity, because the funding conversation tends to place them in the wrong category. When the storm came through my constituency, the power was out across a wide area for the best part of three days. That is a civil protection function being delivered by a commercial entity at its own expense, and we should recognise it as such. The commercial position of these stations is genuinely difficult and getting worse. Advertising revenue that once sustained local newsrooms has migrated to two or three global platforms which contribute nothing to local journalism and are not required to. The result is that the newsroom is the first cost to be cut, so the station survives while the journalism inside it does not, and what remains is automated music with local branding. That is the trajectory unless something changes. There are things we could do. A sound and vision style fund specifically for local news production, with a straightforward application process that a station employing eleven people can actually complete. Recognition of the emergency broadcasting role with funding attached to it. A levy arrangement on the platforms that carry local content without paying for it, which several other countries have now implemented without the sky falling in. And at minimum, an obligation that public information campaigns place a defined proportion of their spend with local media rather than routing it all through national buys, which is a decision entirely within the Government's own control.

I want to explain why this sector in particular cannot simply be left to the general scheme's timetable, because I know the Treasury's instinct is that a universal scheme should end universally and that carve-outs are administratively messy. What the bill requires is measurement by a common method, published in a common format, at a granularity that reflects actual experience rather than aggregate averages. Let me start with what the bill actually does, because the public debate has been conducted largely in terms of what people fear it does. It removes a set of mandatory minimum penalties, principally in relation to certain firearms and drug offences, and it expands the availability of conditional sentences and diversion measures for simple possession. It does not decriminalize anything. It does not prevent a court from imposing a custodial sentence where the circumstances warrant one. A judge retains every power to imprison that they currently possess. What changes is that the judge is no longer required to impose a specific term regardless of the facts before them. I have thought about this a great deal, and I have moved from where I started. The argument for minimums is that they provide certainty, deter offending and remove inconsistency between judges. The evidence on deterrence is, unfortunately for that argument, close to unanimous in the other direction. What deters is the probability of apprehension, not the length of the sentence, and every serious review of the literature finds the same thing. On consistency, minimums do not remove discretion, they relocate it to the prosecutor, who decides which charge to lay, and prosecutorial discretion is exercised without reasons and without appeal. Where I do have reservations is on the firearms provisions, and I will say so plainly even though it is not the position my constituents necessarily expect from me. The offences involved include some genuinely serious conduct, and I want to hear from the minister at committee about how the sentencing outcomes will be monitored. If the result is materially lighter sentences for trafficking offences, that is a problem, and I would want the ability to revisit it. A review clause with a five-year reporting requirement would address my concern.

vaccination, and I agree with that, but vaccination and testing are complements rather than substitutes, and the Government has spent months treating them as alternatives. Let me set out the position we have arrived at. Antigen tests in this State are sold at retail at a price that puts routine use out of reach for a family on a low income. A household of five testing twice weekly faces a meaningful weekly cost. In other member states the same tests are distributed free or at a heavily subsidised price, in some cases through pharmacies, in some cases through schools, and in some cases posted directly to households. The consequence of our approach is entirely predictable and has been measured. Testing rates correlate with income. Which means detection correlates with income. Which means transmission is being suppressed in wealthy areas and not in poor ones, and the case numbers by area reflect exactly that. We have, in effect, means-tested infection control. The Government's earlier objection to antigen testing was a scientific one, that the sensitivity is lower than PCR and that a negative result might produce false reassurance. That was a legitimate concern when it was raised. It has been overtaken by evidence, specifically the finding that sensitivity for infectiousness, as opposed to for the presence of viral material, is considerably higher than the headline figures suggested, and that frequency compensates for sensitivity in a screening context. The expert group's own advice has moved. The policy has moved more slowly, and the gap between the two has been filled by a supply of tests purchased at retail by those who can afford them. I am asking for three specific things. Free distribution through schools for the remainder of this term. A subsidised price cap at retail. And a public information campaign explaining what a negative result does and does not mean, because the false reassurance risk is real and is addressed by explanation, not by scarcity.

Let me explain what I mean by falling at the first hurdle, because it is a specific finding rather than a rhetorical flourish. When researchers submitted a standard set of harmful queries to the major search services, the responses varied enormously between providers, and in several cases returned material that the companies' own published policies said would not be returned. When those results were put to the companies, the response in each case was that the examples were unrepresentative. They may well be. We have no way of knowing, because the underlying data on how frequently such results are served, to whom, and with what refinements, is held exclusively by the companies and disclosed to nobody. That is the hurdle. Not the presence of harmful content, which is to some degree inevitable in a system indexing the whole web, but the refusal to permit any independent measurement of its prevalence. The lawful but harmful category has attracted a great deal of criticism, some of it thoughtful, and I want to engage with the strongest version of it rather than the weakest. The strongest version says that requiring companies to act against lawful speech makes private corporations the arbiters of legitimate expression, that they will over-remove to reduce their own risk, and that the material removed will disproportionately be that of marginal or unpopular voices. I think that is a serious argument. My answer is that the duty as drafted is a duty to assess and to apply one's own terms consistently, not a duty to remove specified content. The regulator does not get to define the harmful category by decree. But I would strengthen the Bill in one respect to meet the objection properly. There should be a statutory route for a user whose content is removed to obtain reasons and to appeal, independently of the platform, because a duty on companies without a corresponding right for users produces exactly the over-removal that critics predict.

It concerns tactics that are deliberately designed to impose maximum disruption on people who have no involvement in the dispute. Gluing oneself to a motorway gantry does not inconvenience a government. I have heard the argument that the suffragettes were disruptive, that the civil rights movement was disruptive, and that history vindicates disruption. It is a serious argument and it deserves a serious answer rather than a dismissive one. My answer is that in each of those cases the protesters were excluded from the political process altogether. They had no vote, no representation, and no lawful means of pursuing their objective. That is not the situation of the organisations we are discussing, whose members can vote, stand for election, petition, litigate, and lobby, and several of whom have done all five with some success. Disruption as a last resort for the disenfranchised is a different moral category from disruption as a first resort by the enfranchised. Where I would accept criticism of the Bill is on the drafting of certain of the wider offences, which are broader than the mischief requires, and which could capture conduct that nobody in this House intends to criminalise. We have created, for one group of arrivals, a scheme with a payment to hosts, a right to work from day one, and access to mainstream services. For another group, fleeing circumstances that are not materially different, we maintain a system of institutional accommodation, no right to work, and a weekly allowance that has not been increased in line with anything. The people in the second category can see the first category. So can their neighbours. the claim that this is a matter of legitimate debate, and that those who object are attempting to shut down discussion. I want to take that argument apart, because it is deployed constantly and it works, and it works because it borrows the language of a genuine liberal principle in order to defeat that principle's purpose. Free expression protects the contest of ideas. It does not require that every proposition be treated as unresolved indefinitely. There are questions that were argued, examined and settled, and reopening them is not inquiry, it is a tactic. The tactic has a recognisable structure. First, insist that a settled matter is an open question. Second, demand equal treatment for both sides of the now-open question. Third, treat any refusal as censorship, thereby converting the refusal into evidence of a conspiracy to suppress. At no point is any evidence required, because the argument is never about evidence. It is about establishing standing, and standing is all that is needed, because once a position is treated as one side of a debate it has already won the only thing it was seeking. The correct response is not prohibition, which supplies the martyrdom the tactic requires, and I want to be clear about that because I know some colleagues would go further than I would. The correct response is to decline the frame while continuing to state the facts. Do not accept the invitation to debate whether something documented beyond any doubt occurred. Do explain, repeatedly and patiently, why the question is not open, and who benefits from pretending it is. And be alert to the second stage, which follows reliably, in which the same actors move from disputing the historical record to identifying a contemporary group as responsible for its supposed fabrication. That is where this always leads, in every country the hon. Lady mentioned, and the interval between the two stages is shorter than most people expect.
